name: Breadcrumbs
markup: No html in this file. Each variant below carries the path to its own markup at r/breadcrumbs/<variant>.html — fetch the one you need.
description: The path from the section root down to the record on screen. The last crumb says where you are and is not a link.
when_to_use: Any page two or more levels deep. One level deep does not need a trail — it needs a back link, which is the back variant here. A page that is a step in a sequence or a panel over another page is not a location at all, and the sequence variant is what that looks like.
rules: The separator is a slash, always. There is no chevron variant and no icon variant; a trail that reads "Home / Procurement / PO-24-1187" in one file and uses chevrons in another is two components pretending to be one.
The last crumb is plain text with aria-current="page". Making it a link to itself is a dead control, and users click it and get nothing.
Never truncate the last crumb. It is the one that says where you are. Truncate the middle, or collapse it into an overflow menu.
The trail is the information hierarchy, not the browsing history. It does not change based on how the user arrived, so two people on the same record see the same trail.

Where a record has more than one plausible parent — a GRN reachable from the order, from the vendor and from the receipt register — the trail takes the one parent that is the same for everybody and the other routes are written beside it as relationships. A crumb chosen from the referrer is history again, and it is the worst kind: it looks like structure, so it is believed.

A crumb the user may not open is named and not linked. Dropping the level makes the trail claim a depth the record does not have; leaving the link in ships a path whose third step is a 403. The same shape covers a parent that was deleted — the stored label, no href, and one line saying why. Where the label itself is what the permission protects, the crumb reads "Restricted" instead of the name, because naming it leaks exactly the thing that was locked.

Only the levels the route already proves get a placeholder while the record is fetched. A GRN URL proves there is a register above it and a section above that, so those two can wait as bars. Nothing proves how many levels sit above a search result, and guessing draws a trail that is a different length when it lands.

A step in a sequence is not a level, and neither is a dialog. Steps are not addressable, they hold unsaved input, and a crumb promises a page that can be bookmarked and reloaded. The trail on a wizard names the page the wizard is; the step count sits with the title.
Crumbs are not underlined, unlike every other link in the system. Five underlined links in a row is a fence, not a path; the muted colour and the hover carry it instead.

anatomy.description: A <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"> holding an ordered list, because the order is the information and a screen reader needs to be able to skip it.
A link to an ancestor page, text-zinc-600, darkening to zinc-900 on hover.
A zinc-500 slash. Decorative and aria-hidden, so it is never read aloud. zinc-400 is the on-dark step of the text scale and is a shade too light for a mark on white.
Plain text in zinc-900 font-medium, never a link, carrying aria-current="page".
The collapsed middle of a long trail: an ellipsis button and, behind it, a nested ordered list of the levels it hides.
An h-2.5 bg-zinc-200 bar in a one-line box, standing where a label will land that the fetch has not returned yet. Not a link, and aria-hidden, so nothing tabs into a grey rectangle.
A level that exists in the hierarchy but not for this user: the label in zinc-500 behind a lock icon, no href, and the reason written on the page under the trail.
The other records this one belongs to, under the trail and labelled — ordinary underlined links, so nothing there is mistaken for a level.
Anything that belongs to the record rather than the page — a status pill, a copy-id button. They sit outside the <ol> entirely, beside the nav, never inside the last <li>.

behaviour: The last crumb is the current page and is not a link. A link to the page you are on is a dead control.
The last crumb is never truncated or collapsed — it is the one that says where you are.
A long trail collapses its middle into an overflow menu rather than wrapping onto two lines.
Below sm the trail collapses to the parent and the current page. Four crumbs at 390px either wrap or push the page sideways, and both are worse than showing two.
The trail reflects the hierarchy, not the history, so it does not change based on how the user arrived.
Crumb labels match the titles of the pages they point at, so following one is not a surprise.

While the parents are in flight, everything the page already knows is drawn for real — the root, and the record number that came out of the URL. Only the labels that are actually waiting are bars, and the trail reflows when they land while the title under it does not move.
A crumb with no href is inert to the pointer and to the keyboard. It does not hover, it does not focus, and it is not a tab stop, because there is nowhere for it to go.
When the page content is swapped without a page load, the trail is swapped with it. A trail left behind by an htmx swap is wrong and silent about it, which is worse than a trail that is missing.
accessibility: A <nav> with aria-label="Breadcrumb", so assistive technology can identify it and skip past it.
An ordered list inside, because the sequence carries the meaning.
Separators are aria-hidden, or a screen reader reads "slash" between every crumb.
The current page carries aria-current="page" — that, not the styling, is what announces it.
The overflow button has an aria-label naming how many levels it hides, because an ellipsis says nothing on its own.

The overflow panel is a list of links and carries no role="menu". role="menu" promises the menu keyboard model — arrows between items, Home and End, one tab stop for the set — and a panel of plain anchors delivers none of it. Links in a list are already navigable; take the role and the browser stops treating them as links.

Crumb links declare the same focus outline as every other control in the system: focus-visible:outline-3 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-zinc-700/15. The trail is often the first thing under the skip link, so it is the first place a keyboard lands on a record page, and leaving it to the user agent means the indicator changes between browsers on the one control that is guaranteed to be reached by keyboard.

While the trail is loading, aria-busy sits on the <nav> and the placeholder crumbs are aria-hidden, with one sr-only role="status" naming the record outside them. Read out, a bar is an empty list item, and three of them is a trail that appears to have lost its labels.
A crumb that is not a link says so in text — an sr-only clause after the label — rather than in the lock icon, which is aria-hidden, or in the grey, which is not announced at all.
